items.title: Justifying the design of ai interventions in education: An analysis of teachers’ attitudes and a multi-layered readiness model
items.abstract: Introduction. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into general secondary education is accompanied by a persistent gap between teachers’ declared readiness to use AI tools and their actual integration into the learning process. Teachers employ AI primarily for routine tasks, while its potential for transforming instruction and personalization remains unrealized, creating risks of cognitive debt for students and the erosion of professional agency. The lack of empirically grounded models for designing AI interventions that account for teachers’ attitudes and cognitive risks impedes pedagogically sound AI integration. This study aims to empirically substantiate a two-axis ‘cognitive offloading – agency’ model and a four-layer ‘AI Readiness – 4L’ model based on an empirical analysis of teachers’ attitudes, practices, and barriers to AI use, as well as to formulate architectural principles for AI interventions. Materials and Methods. The theoretical framework comprised a synthesis of the ‘Systems AI Readiness’ concept, the SAMR, SCOT, JTBD, and TPACK models, and Bandura’s social cognitive theory. The empirical basis was a mixed-method design (2024–2025) conducted across four comprehensive secondary schools in Tomsk (Russia). The quantitative component involved a survey of teachers (n=118); the qualitative component included interviews with school principals (n=3). Thematic analysis and case study methods were employed. Results. A ‘readiness paradox’ was identified: despite positive attitudes toward AI, less than a third of teachers regularly use AI tools, and the majority rate their AI competencies as insufficient. Differentiation in principals’ managerial positions was established. A two-axis ‘cognitive offloading – agency’ model with four types of interaction in the «student – AI – teacher» system was empirically substantiated. The critical risk of cognitive debt occurs when high offloading is combined with low agency. A four-layer ‘AI Readiness – 4L’ model (technological, social, needs-based, and competency layers) was developed. Social-organizational factors, rather than infrastructure, were found to be the key predictors of readiness. Architectural principles for AI interventions were formulated. The critical risk of cognitive debt occurs when high offloading is combined with low agency. A four-layer ‘AI Readiness – 4L’ model (technological, social, needs-based, and competency layers) was developed. Social-organizational factors, rather than infrastructure, were found to be the key predictors of readiness. Architectural principles for AI interventions were formulated. Conclusions. The proposed models and principles provide a foundation for designing AI interventions that leverage the transformative potential of technology while preserving teacher agency and student cognitive autonomy, confirming the necessity of transitioning to pedagogically mediated AI adoption.

items.title: La imagen proyectual: promptografías y agencia visual en el diseño
items.abstract: AI-generated images produced by generative artificial intelligence (GAI) appear to be altering the conditions under which ideas emerge in the design process. However, research on their cognitive effects during ideation remains fragmented and, at times, contradictory. This article does not present original empirical research; rather, its contribution is based on a critical and interpretive review of recent academic literature (2023-2025) on generative images, visual agency, and ideation in design and architecture. These images are examined as external supports of design thinking, in continuity with the graphic representations studied by Schön (1983) and Cross (2006), and read through the lens of distributed and extended cognition (Hutchins, 1995; Clark and Chalmers, 1998). The corpus was selected according to its relevance to three key issues: the cognitive function of GAI-generated images as supports for formal exploration, lateral thinking, and metacognition; the role of unexpected variations and “creative errors” as catalysts, or as sources of visual fixation, in design thinking; and the redistribution of creative agency imposed by these systems, shifting the act of design from execution toward selection, curation, and the critical reading of algorithmic output. The concept of the projective image is proposed to designate those generative images that do not translate a prior idea but instead constitute the site where the idea emerges. The review shows that GAI simultaneously produces thematic expansion and stylistic convergence, and that its effect on creativity depends more on the level of critical judgment exercised by the designer over the output than on the degree of intervention. The article argues that the productive integration of GAI into the design process requires an active critical stance toward the agency of the generated image.

items.title: Model Kepemimpinan Transformasional dalam Meningkatkan Motivasi Intrinsik dan Mengelola Stres Kerja Perawat Rumah Sakit
items.abstract: Background: Nurses serve as the primary drivers of hospital healthcare services; however, high workloads and emotional pressures place them at risk for occupational stress. Transformational leadership is proposed as a managerial style capable of fostering intrinsic motivation and reducing nurse stress levels. Objective: This study aimed to analyze the relationship between transformational leadership, intrinsic motivation, and occupational stress among hospital nurses, while testing the mediating role of intrinsic motivation. Methods: A quantitative study with a cross-sectional design was conducted among 107 active nurses selected through purposive sampling. Data collection instruments included the Global Transformational Leadership Scale (GTL), an Intrinsic Motivation scale based on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and an Occupational Stress scale based on the Job Demand-Control model. Data analysis comprised descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and mediation analysis via the Baron & Kenny approach, Sobel test, and bootstrapping. Results: Most nurses perceived transformational leadership (4.08 ± 0.52) and intrinsic motivation (4.13 ± 0.36) at high levels, with occupational stress at a moderate level (2.93 ± 0.39). Transformational leadership positively correlated with intrinsic motivation (r = 0.642, p < 0.001) and negatively correlated with job stress (r = -0.323, p < 0.001). Mediation analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation fully mediated the relationship between transformational leadership and job stress (Sobel Z = -2.816, p = 0.0049; 68.9% indirect effect). Conclusion: Transformational leadership reduces nurse job stress indirectly by strengthening intrinsic motivation. Hospital nurse managers should adopt leadership practices focused on supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness to foster sustainable healthcare environments.

items.title: Operational Epistemic Situational Awareness in Agentic Orchestration
items.abstract: Long-running agent workflows can lose task scope, source custody, authority, current environment state, unresolved conflicts, or knowledge of what another worker is doing. Operational Epistemic Situational Awareness (ESA) is proposed as the capability to maintain and query an evidence-qualified model of those conditions and to govern continuation when that model becomes stale, conflicted, missing, or outside authority. The architecture uses a governed meaning substrate as an orchestration sidecar, but a sidecar is not awareness by itself. Agent check-ins can be false or stale; receipts can record claims without proving effects; exclusive task claims can deadlock; handoffs can be unaccepted; and unmediated tools can bypass the substrate. The system must distinguish asserted, observed, inferred, stale, conflicted, and unknown state; combine voluntary reports with independent observations; preserve liveness and recovery; and govern sensitive operational data. This paper defines an operational state model, check-in and claim leases, accepted handoff capsules, evidence postures, refusal and escalation outcomes, bypass and availability conditions, cold-boot orientation through the Governed Meaning Base, realization funnel, and comparative evaluation. It makes no claim of consciousness or privileged agent self-knowledge.

items.title: Pemanfaatan Artificial Intelligence Dalam Deteksi Dini, Early Warning System, dan Sistem Rujukan Kegawatdaruratan Pada Resource-Limited Settings: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Background: Healthcare facilities with limited resources face various challenges in early detection and emergency referral systems, including shortages of healthcare personnel, inadequate infrastructure, and the limited accuracy of conventional screening methods. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to serve as a solution to improve the quality of clinical decision-making under these conditions. Objective: This scientific paper aims to identify and synthesize current evidence regarding the use of AI in early detection, early warning systems, and triage. Methods: This study is a narrative review using the PubMed and Google Scholar databases. English-language articles published between 2019 and 2026 that discussed the implementation of AI in early detection or emergency referral systems in resource-limited settings were included. Of the 2,376 articles identified, 16 met the inclusion criteria. Results: The articles were predominantly focused on early detection and early warning systems (50%), followed by triage and referral systems (31%), and health system strengthening (19%). Machine Learning and Deep Learning were the most commonly used AI methods. Several studies demonstrated high performance, with AUC values ranging from 0.80 to 0.97. AI was shown to improve the accuracy of sepsis detection, patient prioritization, and support faster and more objective referral decision-making. Conclusion: AI has the potential to enhance early detection, triage, and emergency referral systems in healthcare facilities with limited resources, although its implementation continues to face challenges related to infrastructure, user trust, as well as regulatory and data governance aspects.

items.title: PEMANFAATAN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DALAM PENGINJILAN DIGITAL BAGIGENERASI Z MELALUI MEDIA SOSIAL:KAJIAN TEOLOGIS
items.abstract: Abstrak Tujuan penelitian ini adalah untuk mengkaji pemanfaatan Artificial Intelligence (AI) secara teologis sebagai sarana pendukung penginjilan digital bagi Generasi Z melalui media sosial. Perkembangan AI dan media sosial telah mengubah cara Generasi Z berkomunikasi, memperoleh informasi, membangun relasi, dan berinteraksi dengan pesan-pesan keagamaan. Perubahan tersebut memberikan peluang baru bagi gereja untuk memberitakan Injil melalui berbagai platform digital, sekaligus menghadirkan tantangan teologis dan etis berkaitan dengan autentisitas, tanggung jawab manusia, otoritas Kitab Suci, pengaruh algoritma, dan dimensi relasional dalam penginjilan. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode kualitatif deskriptif melalui studi kepustakaan terhadap berbagai kajian teologis, misiologis, dan interdisipliner mengenai AI, teologi digital, media sosial, Generasi Z, dan penginjilan Kristen. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa AI dapat mendukung penginjilan digital melalui produksi konten, penerjemahan, personalisasi pesan, pengembangan visual, dan perluasan jangkauan pemberitaan Injil. Namun, AI tidak dapat menggantikan manusia sebagai saksi Kristus karena tidak memiliki iman, pengalaman spiritual, tanggung jawab moral, dan kehadiran relasional sebagaimana manusia. Oleh karena itu, AI perlu ditempatkan sebagai sarana misi, bukan subjek misi. Kristus tetap menjadi pusat Injil, Kitab Suci menjadi dasar pemberitaan, manusia menjadi saksi, AI berfungsi sebagai sarana pendukung, media sosial menjadi ruang komunikasi dan perjumpaan, sedangkan arah akhir penginjilan digital adalah terbentuknya relasi dan pemuridan. Kata-kata kunci: Artificial Intelligence, penginjilan digital, Generasi Z, media sosial, teologi digital, pemuridan abstract The purpose of this study is to examine the theological use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a supporting medium for digital evangelism among Generation Z through social media. The rapid development of AI and social media has transformed the way Generation Z communicates, obtains information, builds relationships, and encounters religious messages. This transformation provides new opportunities for the church to proclaim the gospel through digital platforms, while also raising theological and ethical challenges concerning authenticity, human responsibility, biblical authority, algorithmic influence, and the relational nature of evangelism. This study employs a descriptive qualitative method through a literature review of theological, missiological, and interdisciplinary studies concerning AI, digital theology, social media, Generation Z, and Christian evangelism. The findings indicate that AI can support digital evangelism through content production, translation, personalization, visual development, and wider dissemination of gospel messages. However, AI cannot replace human beings as witnesses of Christ because it does not possess faith, spiritual experience, moral responsibility, or relational presence. Therefore, AI should be positioned as a means of mission rather than a subject of mission. Christ remains the center of the gospel, Scripture remains the foundation of its message, human beings remain witnesses, AI functions as a supporting tool, social media becomes a space for communication and encounter, and the ultimate direction of digital evangelism is relationship and discipleship. Key words: Artificial Intelligence, digital evangelism, Z Generation, social media, digital theology, discipleship

items.title: Philosophy, Ethics and Artificial Intelligence a Human-Centred Framework for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has developed from a specialised area of computer science into a general-purpose technology that increasingly influences education, healthcare, finance, employment, communication, governance and everyday decision-making. This expansion makes AI not only a technological subject but also a philosophical and ethical concern. This conceptual research paper examines the relationship between philosophy, ethics and artificial intelligence from a human-centred perspective. It analyses the ethical significance of human dignity, autonomy, privacy, justice, fairness, transparency, accountability, responsibility and sustainability. The study uses qualitative conceptual analysis of philosophical literature, AI ethics scholarship and major institutional frameworks. Particular attention is given to deontological ethics, consequentialism, virtue ethics and selected Indian ethical ideas. The paper further examines algorithmic bias, surveillance, opacity, manipulation, employment transformation, education, environmental impact and the problem of assigning responsibility for AI-mediated decisions. Contemporary frameworks of UNESCO, OECD, NIST and NITI Aayog are examined as important attempts to translate ethical principles into governance and risk-management practices. The analysis indicates that responsible AI cannot be achieved by technical safeguards alone. Ethical reasoning needs to be integrated across the complete AI lifecycle, from problem formulation and data selection to design, testing, deployment, monitoring and retirement. A human-centred framework is proposed around eight principles: human dignity, human agency, non-maleficence, justice and inclusion, privacy, explainability and contestability, accountability, and sustainability. The paper concludes that the fundamental question for the AI era is not merely what machines can do, but what human purposes, values and limits should guide their development and use.

items.title: Predictors of Motivation for English Language Learning among University Students in Helmand Province, Afghanistan
items.abstract: Although English is taught in Afghan universities, the factors that motivate students in Helmand Province to learn it remain under-researched. This study examined how intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and English learning confidence shape overall motivation to learn English in Helmand Province, Afghanistan. A quantitative correlational design was used to collect data through a structured questionnaire from 324 male students across four universities (Helmand University, Bost University, Arakozia University, and Wadie Helmand University) using multi-stage stratified random sampling. Each construct was measured using five items rated on a 5-point Likert scale. The study used descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, paired-sample t-test, and multiple regression. The results indicated high overall motivational levels (M = 4.39, SD = 0.63), and intrinsic motivation (M = 4.38, SD = 0.53) was significantly higher than extrinsic motivation (M = 3.95, SD = 0.83), t = 10.03, p <. 001. The correlational analysis revealed a significant positive correlation among all variables (p < .001), and English learning confidence had the strongest correlation with overall motivation (r = .623). The multiple regression analysis indicated that the three predictors explained 45.4% of the variance in overall motivation (R2 =.454). The findings suggest that while both intrinsic and extrinsic motivations are important, students in the target universities are highly influenced by internal factors. This study emphasizes the importance of psychological factors in sustaining motivation among university students in Helmand Province.

items.title: Privacy And Data Protection Challenges in The Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) structures rely on large amounts of private records for training and deployment. This creates privacy concerns that common fact safety systems now would not have been designed to handle, along with opaque statistical series, net scraping without meaningful consent, inferences about sensitive features, leakage of training statistics from models, surveillance, and automated decision making. The rapid development of generative AI has heightened those concerns, as fashions that are proficient on internet-scale data currently are used by tens of millions of those who mechanically embed private records into them. It assesses the main legal frameworks, particularly the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the EU AI Act, and India’s Digital Personal Information Protection Act, 2023, and identifies gaps in how they handle inferred facts, educated fashions, and enforcement of erasure rights. It also considers regulatory enforcement enjoy, consisting of actions against Clearview AI and ChatGPT, to show how current regulation is applied to AI in practice. Finally, it evaluates technical security measures consisting of differential privacy and connected knowing, along with organizational measures consisting of privacy-by-design, impact assessments, and independent audits. The paper argues that effective security requires the implementation of legal responsibilities mixed with privacy-preserving engineering, instead of either on my own, and that responsibility should be shifted upstream to people who design, train, and deploy AI systems. It concludes with suggestions for regulators, with special reference to the Indian context.

items.title: Quality of Models in AI
items.abstract: With the extended SEQUAL framework presented in Chap 3 , we can examine aspects of the quality of models for man and machines more systematically. We start with an example of how to assess the quality of symbolic models for human use, building on earlier work using SEQUAL to evaluate ontologies, and extending it to include aspects of the renewed framework. Then we present a case study of a machine learning system in which the quality of the results depends on both symbolic and sub-symbolic models. In Sect. 4.3, we discuss how sustainability considerations are important when selecting ML techniques for data at various points along the pipeline. Section 4.4 ends the chapter by investigating the quality of explanation models in XAI.

items.title: Responsible Management of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Balancing Innovation, Ethics, and Student Well-Being
items.abstract: Abstract Integration of AI in the educational system is rapidly changing the face of education by offering new possibilities of personalized learning and efficient management at the same time creating serious issues related to student autonomy, data security, and psychology. The paper suggests a holistic framework for the management of AI in education by using recommendations for the responsible use of AI in various spheres developed by international organizations like UNESCO together with recent findings about the psychological state of students. We suggest that successful integration of AI into educational practices should be based on a transition from technology-based management of AI to human-based one where student well-being becomes one of the major ethical considerations.

items.title: Revolutionary transformation of digital art:ontological reconstruction and paradigm shift driven by technology
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines changes in digital art’s creative mechanisms, subject relations, and conditions of existence through the lens of the philosophy of technology. Tracing the evolution from mechanical and electronic media to algorithmic systems, the paper argues that technology no longer functions merely as an external tool but increasingly intervenes in artistic cognition, creative processes, and the conditions under which works are generated. The paper outlines three notable dimensions of change in digital art: technologically mediated existence, distributed creative relations, and algorithmically shaped aesthetic processes. The paper also examines three tensions: Western aesthetic dominance via biased training data, NFT-driven value paradoxes, and destabilized artistic subjectivity under generative AI. Drawing on process philosophy, complexity theory, and technological phenomenology, it proposes a techno-cognitive framework positioning digital art as a dynamic interface between technology and human cognition. The study proposes evaluative and ethical discussion frameworks better suited to contemporary digital art, with the aim of supporting further theoretical analysis.

items.title: Social and Pedagogical Drivers of ChatGPT Acceptance: An Extended TAM Model in Teacher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tools, particularly applications such as ChatGPT, hold significant potential to reshape the landscape of teacher education by offering opportunities for personalized feedback and adaptive learning. These tools also play important roles in teachers’ pedagogical decisions while designing their teachings in present learning environments. However, the underlying mechanisms driving pre-service teachers’ adoption of such particular tools remain under-explored. This study addresses this gap by validating an extended technology acceptance model incorporating constructivist teaching beliefs, subjective norms, facilitating conditions, ChatGPT self-efficacy, and perceived enjoyment. Data collected from 488 senior pre-service teachers in Türkiye were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that ChatGPT self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment significantly predict perceived ease of use, whereas facilitating conditions do not exert a significant influence. Perceived usefulness is significantly associated with perceived ease of use, subjective norms, and pedagogical beliefs. Behavioral intention is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norms, and ChatGPT self-efficacy, with the framework explaining 54% of the variance. Given the cross-sectional nature of the data, these results offer tentative implications for teacher education. Practically, the findings highlight the potential value of scaffolded micro-teaching and institutional verification procedures for supporting responsible and equitable generative AI use in teacher education. Further recommendations are discussed in the light of teacher education procedures and policies.

items.title: Sustained use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in programming education: a systematic review of empirical evidence on adoption, learning outcomes, and continuance intention
items.abstract: This systematic review explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies have been adopted and sustained within programming education from 2023 to 2025, uncovering their applications, educational benefits, and challenges. This review draws on 45 empirical studies identified through five major academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. The analysis reveals that GenAI could enhance programming education by supporting code generation, debugging assistance, personalised explanations, feedback provision, and learner engagement. However, key challenges remain concerning inaccurate outputs, academic integrity, learner dependency, trust, and unequal access to AI-supported learning resources. This study suggests that educators should strategically employ GenAI as a complementary learning resource, maximising its educational benefits while addressing potential limitations. The findings highlight the importance of educator preparation, institutional guidance, and responsible AI integration, while future research should further investigate long-term continuance intention behaviour, comparative effectiveness of emerging GenAI programming tools, and sustainable implementation strategies across diverse educational contexts.

items.title: Task Context Shapes Ocular Associations with Stress, Cognitive Workload, and Fatigue: A Wearable Eye-Tracking Study
items.abstract: Background: Eye-tracking correlations with cognitive and emotional states vary across studies, likely because they depend on specific task demands. We investigated the consistency and specificity of such associations between wearable eye-tracking data and self-reported measures of stress, cognitive workload, and fatigue within assessment-centre-style tasks.Methods: Participants performed tasks involving social evaluation, reasoning, planning, comprehension, and presentation while wearing Meta Aria Gen 1 glasses. Data from 97 participants were analysed using linear mixed-effects models to examine associations between 104 wearable eye-tracking and head-movement metrics and each self-reported state, while accounting for task effects. Metric-by-task interactions assessed task dependence, and sensitivity analyses examined the effects of elapsed session time and shared variance among states.Results: After false-discovery-rate correction, significant metric-by-task interactions were observed in 53 stress, 61 workload, and 12 fatigue models, especially for saccade amplitude, speed, and duration. Across tasks, stress was linked to increased gaze variability, while workload and fatigue were linked to greater fixation angular distance. Fatigue associations weakened after adjusting for session time, and no fatigue metric-by-task interactions remained significant after adjustment for elapsed session time. After controlling for overlap among self-reported states, associations remained significant for stress, but not workload or fatigue.Conclusion: Ocular associations varied by task and by the shared variance across subjective states. Measures of fixation distribution appeared to capture a more general subjective-state component rather than exclusively distinguishing workload or fatigue. Several gaze and saccade associations with stress remained significant after adjustment for workload and fatigue. Predictive modelling should distinguish shared from state-specific information and be validated across diverse activities.

items.abstract: This study examined the classroom and instructional management practices of new and experienced teachers and their relationship with students’ learning engagement in selected public secondary schools in Cortes District, Division of Bohol, during School Year 2026–2027. Anchored in the Classroom Management Scripts Model, Instructional Clarity Framework, Multidimensional Student Engagement Framework, and Huberman’s Teacher Career Cycle, the study employed a quantitative comparative-correlational research design. Respondents comprised 15 new teachers, 46 experienced teachers, and 278 students, totaling 339 participants. Data were gathered using a researcher-modified, validated, and pilot-tested questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson product–moment correlation, and independent-samples t-tests. Results revealed consistently high classroom and instructional management practices among both teacher groups, with no statistically significant differences. Classroom management and instructional management exhibited a strong positive relationship (r = 0.724, p < 0.001), whereas neither classroom management (r = 0.040, p = 0.760) nor instructional management (r = −0.062, p = 0.635) was significantly associated with students’ overall learning engagement. Students taught by new teachers demonstrated significantly higher overall and emotional engagement (p = 0.017), while behavioral and cognitive engagement showed no significant differences. The study concluded that teaching experience alone does not determine management effectiveness and that favorable management practices do not necessarily correspond to higher student engagement. A school-based professional development program emphasizing mentoring, collaborative lesson planning, peer observation, and instructional improvement was proposed. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting effective teaching, inclusive learning environments, and continuous professional growth. Its educational and institutional sustainability contribution lies in providing localized evidence to guide sustained professional development and improvements in students’ learning experiences.

items.title: Technology acceptance mediates associations between pre-service physical education teachers’ AI-TPACK and study engagement and behavioral intentions in digital teaching
items.abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of artificial intelligence (AI) reshaping the educational landscape, the digital transformation of physical education has placed greater demands on preservice physical education teachers’ (PSPETs’) capacity to integrate technology. However, research remains limited on the effects of pres-ervice physical education teachers’ artificial intelligence technological pedagogical content knowledge (PSPETs AI-TPACK) on their study engagement (SE) and behavioral intentions (BI) in digital teaching, as well as on the role played by technology acceptance (TA) in these relationships.This study involved 1,144 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in physical education, physical education teaching, or physical education and training programmes at five higher education institutions in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province. Using adapted scales, data were collected on PSPETs AI-TPACK, TA, SE, and BI. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was then employed to examine the relationships among these variables and the mediating effects. The findings showed that PSPETs AI-TPACK significantly and positively predicted both SE and BI in digital teaching. TA played a significant partial mediating role in the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE, and between PSPETs AI-TPACK and BI. These results indicate that PSPETs AI-TPACK can promote PSPETs’ SE and BI both directly and indirectly by enhancing their TA. This study extends the theoretical understanding of the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE and BI in digital physical education teaching, while also providing empirical evidence for improving preservice physical education teacher education in higher education institutions. Higher education institutions should incorporate AI-based instructional design and practice into physical education teacher education curricula, implement tiered and progressive technology training, create authentic digital teaching contexts, and enhance PSPETs’ TA through resource provision and exemplary applications. These measures can, in turn, strengthen PSPETs’ SE and BI in using AI technologies to support physical education teaching.

items.abstract: THE ALGORITHMIC SKINNER BOX: A PHCA SYSTEMS AUDIT OF REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULES, COMPUTATIONAL ARCHITECTURE, AND COGNITIVE AUTONOMY Executive Summary & Abstract For nearly a century, B.F. Skinner’s theory of operant conditioning has shaped our understanding of human behavior. The core premise is simple: behavior is shaped by consequences—rewards and punishments. But in the modern era, the environment shaping human behavior is no longer a physical laboratory. It is an adaptive, algorithmic architecture. This paper proposes the Algorithmic Skinner Box as a systems-level model to examine the precise interaction between digital reinforcement schedules, algorithmic personalization, and the measurable degradation of human autonomy. We do not assume that all digital platforms universally produce neurochemical addiction. Instead, we distinguish between specific mechanisms of behavioral conditioning. We analyze the difference between Variable-Ratio (VR) schedules (reinforcement after an unpredictable number of actions), Variable-Interval (VI) schedules (reinforcement after unpredictable time intervals), and the complex Mixed Schedules utilized by modern social media and digital feeds. By applying the Proclean Hierarchical Constraint Architecture (PHCA), we map how adaptive computational systems observe user behavior, modify subsequent stimuli, and optimize engagement through continuous feedback loops. This is the Dioptopticon—an architecture of attention capture that operates without the need for physical coercion. However, this paper explicitly separates observable behavioral conditioning from unverified neurobiological claims. We do not assert that dopamine is a simple "pleasure chemical" being hijacked. Instead, we map dopaminergic reward prediction errors and motivational salience, proposing a rigorous research program to determine exactly how externally controlled reinforcement contingencies alter behavioral response frequency and attentional allocation. The Dynamic System Model To formalize this, we abandon the static metaphors of the past and model the human-algorithm interaction as a dynamic state-space system. We identify four measurable variables: · Attentional Allocation · Compulsive Engagement Frequency · Intrinsic Motivational Orientation · Behavioral Response Sensitivity to External Reinforcement This model defines the platform not as a passive tool, but as a coupled computational system that interacts with the human nervous system in real-time. The Falsification Protocol This is a scientific audit, not a conspiracy theory. The paper proposes five falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H5) to empirically test the effects of these reinforcement schedules. We demand longitudinal testing of executive function, rigorous measurement of withdrawal-related distress, and controlled experiments comparing voluntary engagement against algorithmic compulsion. If traditional behavioral economics explains these phenomena better than the PHCA model, the math must yield to the evidence. Sovereign Cognition: The Architectural Reform We cannot solve algorithmic capture with simple "dopamine detoxes." We must fundamentally redefine psychological autonomy. This paper introduces Sovereign Cognition as an operational construct: Sovereign Cognition is the measurable capacity of an individual to initiate, sustain, interrupt, and redirect goal-directed behavior independently of externally imposed reinforcement contingencies. To restore cognitive sovereignty, we must measure and architect for four dimensions: the ability to Initiate a self-selected task, the ability to Persist in the face of distraction, the ability to Interrupt external stimuli, and the ability to Redirect attention based on internal goals. The Bottom Line A digital system should not be evaluated solely by how effectively it captures attention, but by whether its users retain the ability to withdraw that attention voluntarily. The legacy system engineered a Skinner Box in your pocket. The PHCA framework provides the tools to measure the constraints, expose the feedback loops, and engineer a sovereign way out. The signal is not absolute. The evidence determines its strength. Solve et coagula. — Anthony J. Blair Founder, Proclus Dynamics Consortium

items.title: THE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REVOLUTION IN FINANCE: FROM ALGORITHMS TO STRATEGIC SOLUTIONS
items.abstract: A rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is transforming the financial sector, changing approaches to automating operations, analyzing data bulk, forecasting, risk management, customer service, and making management decisions. The relevance of the study is due to the need to transition from the fragmented and predominantly operational use of algorithmic tools to their systemic integration into strategic management in finance. The purpose of the study is to systematize the areas of application of AI in the financial sector and substantiate the conceptual model of the transition from the operational use of algorithmic tools to the strategic level of management. To achieve the set goal, systemic, historical-logical, comparative, and classification methods were used. The main results of the study are the identification of four stages of the evolution of AI applications in finance: algorithmic-rule, machine learning, deep learning, and generative-strategic. The key areas of AI use are systematized by the level of managerial influence - from the automation of routine operations and support of individual business processes to forecasting, risk management, personalization of financial services, and the formation of strategic management decisions. The technological, regulatory, reputational, ethical, and systemic risks associated with scaling AI in the financial sector are summarized. A five-level maturity model of AI application is proposed, which involves a sequential transition from experimental, operational, and integrated levels to the level of managerial transformation and strategic use of technologies.It is concluded that the strategic value of AI is determined not by the number of implemented technological solutions, but by the degree of their integration into the corporate governance system, the quality and availability of data, the effectiveness of model management, personnel competencies, the explainability of algorithmic solutions, compliance with regulatory requirements, and the effectiveness of risk control. The strategic integration of AI creates the prerequisites for increasing the adaptability, competitiveness, and sustainability of the financial sector.

items.abstract: The Changing Role of Higher Education Leadership in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Longitudinal Qualitative Study How have higher education institutions responded to artificial intelligence between 2022 and 2026? This study examines changes in higher education leadership responses to AI through publicly available institutional policies, guidelines, governance reports, and strategic communications from 11 universities. It considers institutional responses across four analytical periods: emergence, adaptation, integration, and institutionalization. The study contributes to higher education leadership research by examining how institutional AI guidance has developed and how universities have addressed academic integrity, ethical use, AI literacy, teaching and learning, and institutional governance. I welcome researchers, educators, and higher education professionals to read, share, and engage with this study.

items.title: THE USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BASED ON THE CIDI-PROMPTING MODEL TO ENHANCE THE LEVEL OF COGNITIVE COMPETENCIES AND CREATIVE THINKING OF UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical models capable of directing it towards higher-order learning. Unstructured, zero-shot interaction with Large Language Models tends to yield fluent but uncritical output, while conventional assessment instruments are not designed to capture the quality of a learner's interaction with an AI system. This article addresses that gap by presenting the design of a Personalized Multi-Agent System (MAS) built upon the CIDI (Clarify, Ideate, Develop, Implement) pedagogical framework, together with the assessment architecture required to evaluate it. Following a design-based research methodology, four components are specified. First, the CIDI framework is articulated as a four-stage model of structured human-AI interaction, grounded in Distributed Cognition Theory and Cognitive Load Theory. Second, a dual-agent architecture is specified in full: an Ideation Agent configured for divergent generation and a Critical Evaluator Agent configured for convergent methodological critique, each defined by its system prompt and temperature configuration, and both integrated into an institutional Learning Management System. Third, a complete instructional design is presented, implementing the framework as a four-stage research-planning task within a research methodology curriculum, and introducing the Iterative Refinement Cycle (IRC) as an observable indicator of dialogic engagement recoverable from LMS logs. Fourth, two purpose-built assessment instruments are introduced: a 100-point Cognitive Competence Score rubric addressing problem formulation, methodological rigour, logical structuring and academic literacy; and an analytic rubric operationalizing Torrance's four dimensions of divergent thinking. The article concludes with a validation protocol specifying the design, reliability indices and analytic procedures required for subsequent empirical testing. The contribution is methodological: it supplies a reproducible architecture and a transparent instrumentation set for research on structured human-AI interaction in higher education.

items.title: Türkiye’s Vision for Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Document Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping the structure and pedagogy of contemporary education systems. This study examines Türkiye’s strategic vision and institutional orientations toward AI in education by analyzing official policy documents and mapping their theoretical foundations within a structured conceptual framework. This study employed a qualitative document analysis design, examining 14 policy documents, strategic plans, ethical guidelines, and curriculum documents published by the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye, the Ministry of National Education, the Council of Higher Education, and TÜBİTAK between 2021 and 2029. The data were analyzed using thematic content analysis, and the documents were thematically coded using NVivo. The findings indicate that official education policy documents frame AI as a multidimensional paradigm shaped by institutional priorities. AI integration is presented as a predominantly top-down process, with official documents emphasizing advanced engineering applications for secondary education and gifted students, while AI applications for preschool and primary education receive comparatively less attention. AI is portrayed as a tool that supports instructional design while reducing teachers’ administrative and academic workload. At the same time, the ‘human-in-the-loop’ principle is identified as a core safeguard within the national policy framework. The analysis also reveals a restrictive approach to the use of AI in academic assessment. Based on these findings, the study proposes several policy recommendations. These include integrating age-appropriate AI activities into primary education curricula, establishing standardized data anonymization principles to protect student information, and redesigning pre-service and in-service teacher education through practice-oriented professional development aligned with teachers’ evolving roles.

items.title: Weak-Signal Intelligence: An AI-Enabled Intelligent Modeling Framework for Early Detection of Strategic Disruptions
items.abstract: Strategic environments are increasingly characterized by uncertainty, rapid technological change, and disruptions that may initially appear as low-visibility or ambiguous signals. Existing approaches to weak-signal analysis, strategic foresight, early-warning systems, and artificial intelligence address parts of this challenge but remain fragmented, particularly in connecting signal detection with interpretation and strategic assessment. This study develops Weak-Signal Intelligence (WSI) as an AI-enabled organizational capability for detecting, interpreting, integrating, and evaluating weak signals to anticipate emerging strategic disruptions. Using a conceptual theory-building and intelligent modeling approach, the study integrates insights from weak-signal research, strategic foresight, early-warning systems, artificial intelligence, sensemaking, uncertainty, and complexity. The proposed framework connects signal detection, interpretation, pattern recognition, uncertainty analytics, disruption assessment, strategic response intelligence, and adaptive learning. The model positions WSI as a continuous human–AI process that transforms low-visibility signals into uncertainty-aware strategic early-warning intelligence. The study contributes a conceptual foundation for improving strategic awareness and preparedness and provides directions for future empirical validation, measurement development, and cross-sector application.

items.title: Web-Based and Mobile AI Tools in Southeast Asian Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis
items.abstract: Web-based and mobile artificial intelligence tools have spread rapidly in Southeast Asian universities, yet evidence on what they achieved in real learning remained fragmented. This systematic review synthesised empirical studies that implemented or evaluated such tools in degree-level higher education in Southeast Asia between 2021 and 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guideline, 642 Scopus records were screened, 79 full texts were assessed and 59 studies were included. Study quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, measured outcomes were summarised by effect direction, and findings were integrated through three-stage thematic synthesis. Most studies came from Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand, concerned language learning, used general-purpose chatbots and relied on non-randomised designs. Of 45 studies that measured learning, 36 reported improvements, mainly in uncontrolled designs or against routine teaching, whereas four of six comparisons with equivalent human support found no difference. Five analytical themes emerged: polished products with uncertain learning, pedagogy over presence, an affective double edge, unequal readiness and comparator-dependent conclusions. The evidence supported these tools as comparable and scalable complements within teacher-mediated, bounded designs rather than as superior replacements. The review proposed an orchestration framework and a research agenda that prioritised active comparators and independent, delayed measures of learning.

items.title: When Algorithms Set Prices: Emerging Consumer Fairness Challenges in AI-Driven Dynamic Pricing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is turning dynamic pricing from a standardized management decision into an individual, algorithmic experience. Algorithmic pricing improves efficiency and personalization, but its opacity and individualized prices can leave consumers feeling treated unfairly and distrustful. This short communication draws on recent research on algorithmic pricing, price fairness, price transparency, and consumer trust to build a conceptual framework. It links four features of algorithmic pricing (real-time adaptation, personalization, individualized price differentiation, and limited explainability) to perceived price fairness, which in turn shapes consumer trust and acceptance or resistance. The paper argues that fairness is a strategic management problem, not only an ethical concern. Implications for pricing managers cover price explanations, responsible personalization, and governance, and empirical research directions are proposed.

items.title: Work-Related Burnout, Insomnia, and Psychological Well-Being among Computer Programmers: A Correlational Study in Lahore, Pakistan
items.abstract: Background: Computer programmers face intensive cognitive demands, sustained concentration, tight deadlines, and extended working hours that may compromise occupational health. This study examined relationships among work-related burnout, insomnia, and psychological well-being among computer programmers in Lahore, Pakistan. Methods: A cross-sectional correlational study recruited 250 employed programmers, comprising 143 men and 107 women, aged 18–35 years. Data were collected between April and June 2024 through face-to-face questionnaires and Google Forms. Participants completed the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, Bergen Insomnia Scale, and Psychological Well-Being Scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, simple linear regression, and independent-samples t tests in SPSS 23. Results: Burnout correlated positively with insomnia (r = .248, p < .01) and negatively with psychological well-being (r = −.159, p < .05). The insomnia–well-being correlation was nonsignificant (r = −.053, p = .401). Burnout explained 6.2% of insomnia variance and 2.5% of psychological well-being variance. Women reported significantly higher burnout (p = .005) and insomnia (p = .022) than men; their psychological well-being scores did not differ significantly (p = .108). Conclusion: Greater burnout was associated with more insomnia symptoms and modestly poorer psychological well-being among programmers. Occupational workload management and access to employee support deserve attention. Because this study was cross-sectional and relied on self-report measures, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships.

items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) models such as ChatGPT and Gemini, opening new prospects for supporting the educational process. This study aims to measure the effectiveness of generative AI models in improving university students' academic writing skills, using a quasi-experimental design with experimental and control groups (N = 60 second-year students of the Faculty of Education, randomly assigned to the two groups). The experimental group received a six-week training program that integrated generative AI as a writing assistant across brainstorming, drafting, language revision, and referencing, while the control group followed traditional instruction. An academic writing skills test and an observation checklist were used as instruments. The study hypothesizes statistically significant differences (α = 0.05) favoring the experimental group in thesis clarity, idea organization, linguistic accuracy, and academic referencing, alongside positive attitudes toward AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for thinking. In addition, an exploratory descriptive survey of 87 university students found that 93.1% had previously used generative AI tools for academic writing, 95.4% supported clear university policies governing their use, and 72.4% reported concern about over-reliance on them. The study recommends training faculty members to integrate generative AI tools into academic writing courses and establishing an ethical charter to govern their use.

items.title: A CRITICAL REVIEW ON DIGITAL HR TRANSFORMATION AND EMPLOYEE ENGAGEMENT IN THE ERA OF INDUSTRY 5.0
items.abstract: The shift from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0 marks a profound paradigm evolution in strategic human resource management (HRM), transitioning from pure technological automation to human-centric socio-technical synergy, sustainability, and organizational resilience. This critical review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature published between 2021 and 2026 to evaluate the influence of digital HR transformation—encompassing artificial intelligence, predictive people analytics, cloud-based HRIS, and collaborative robotics (cobots)—on multi-dimensional employee engagement (vigor, dedication, and absorption). Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) framework, 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies were systematically selected and categorized. The synthesis reveals that while digital HR transformation significantly drives operational efficiency, its direct impact on employee engagement is mediated by digital fluency, perceived organizational support, and psychological safety. Furthermore, algorithmic transparency and responsible data governance serve as critical moderators that mitigate techno-stress, privacy anxieties, and algorithmic burnout. The paper delivers an integrative socio-technical framework for Industry 5.0, offering strategic guidance for organizational leaders seeking to align cutting-edge HR technologies with human well-being and sustainable performance.

items.title: A CRITICAL REVIEW ON EMPLOYEE WELL-BEING AND SUSTAINABLE HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
items.abstract: In contemporary organizational research, the imperative to balance economic productivity with human sustainability has elevated Sustainable Human Resource Management (Sustainable HRM) into a core strategic framework. This critical review systematically evaluates 16 benchmark empirical and conceptual studies published between 2021 and 2026 to investigate how Sustainable HRM practices influence tri-dimensional employee well-being (physical, psychological, and social) and long-term organizational performance. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocols, this study synthesizes structural equation modelling (SEM) findings, panel econometrics, and qualitative case studies across diverse industrial and geographical settings. The synthesis reveals that while traditional HRM prioritizes short-term transactional output, Sustainable HRM embeds ergonomic work design, psychological safety, work-life boundary protection, and green employee voice, yielding a significant positive effect on psychological capital (β = 0.44, p < .001) and work-family enrichment (β = 0.41, p < .001). Meta-analyzed structural models demonstrate that physical and psychological well-being fully mediate the relationship between sustainable work practices and employee job performance (β = 0.38, p < .001), while drastically reducing turnover intentions. However, critical gaps persist regarding paradoxical workload pressures under green mandates and regional implementation disparities. This paper presents a multi-level governance framework providing actionable pathways for HR leaders to operationalize sustainable well-being.

items.title: A Generative AI-Integrated Framework for Teaching Operations Management: Case-Based Projects
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GAI) reshapes business education, instructors must simultaneously safeguard academic integrity and develop students’ AI literacy for an increasingly AI-driven workplace. This study developed the GAI Learning Framework (GLF), a replicable, step-by-step experiential learning approach for case-based projects in undergraduate business courses, illustrated through an operations management (OM) application. Rather than enabling passive cognitive offloading, the GLF promotes active learning by requiring students to craft context-rich prompts grounded in course materials, systematically compare outputs across multiple GAI platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), and critically evaluate discrepancies against independently verified sources. The framework was implemented across two sections of an undergraduate OM course and evaluated using a student survey that combined Likert-scale items with open-ended reflections (n = 50). All three constructs exceeded the scale midpoint, with pooled means ranging from 3.93 (Constructive Alignment) to 4.08 (Cognitive Load/Scaffolding). Qualitative student reflections further indicated that students perceived the framework as fostering active learning, AI platform literacy, and professional communication skills. This study offers educators a practical, classroom-tested framework for integrating GAI tools into case-based projects in business courses while preserving analytical rigor and promoting experiential learning. items.title: A Plug-and-Play Explainable AI Framework in Credit Score Assessment
items.abstract: Credit scoring is fundamental in enabling institutions to distinguish between creditworthy and high-risk borrowers. Thus, robust credit scoring models are essential for effective financial risk management. Artificial intelligence and machine learning have significantly improved the precision of credit decision support systems, however, these models often operate as black boxes, concealing the underlying logic of credit denials or approvals. To address this challenge and meet the demand for financial transparency, explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a crucial mechanism for generating decisions that are interpretable to both financial institutions and clients. This paper researched contemporary decision support systems (DSS) used in credit risk assessment and proposes a modular, plug-and-play framework with integrated explainability. Six requirements were derived for a robust system design based on a review of existing XAI frameworks. The framework consists of five interconnected components such as data ingestion layer, feature processing module, a supervised predictive model, an explanation layer, and a decision endpoint. Existing studies often focus on individual predictive models or explanation methods, leaving their integration and component interchangeability unspecified. The proposed framework addresses this gap through explicit interfaces that allow predictive models and explanation methods to be replaced independently. The system will operate with both traditional credit data, alternative data, or both. Thus, feature processing is incorporated to distinguish the importance and relevance of the data to credit assessment decisions. Any irrelevant redundant data is not be considered by the model. The contribution of a study is a reusable architectural specification. The proposed XAI framework is designed to serve as a universal template for researchers and financial institutions developing transparent, effective credit scoring systems.

items.title: A Review of Implementation Barriers of Design for Safety (DfS) in the Construction Sector
items.abstract: The construction industry continues to record a high rate of occupational accidents despite sustained safety interventions, indicating that conventional reactive approaches are inadequate. A more proactive approach, such as Design for Safety (DfS), is therefore essential. Although Malaysia introduced the OSHCIM 2017 Guidelines and gazetted the Occupational Safety And Health (Construction Work)(Design and Management) Regulations 2024, which elevated DfS to mandatory status, implementation barriers remain insufficiently classified within a coherent theoretical framework. This study addresses this gap through a narrative synthesis that critically classifies and evaluates DfS barriers, reorganised within the Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory. An analysis of 66 articles from the Scopus and Web of Science databases identifies five (5) barrier clusters: deficiencies in knowledge, education and competency; legal, policy and liability issues; weaknesses in stakeholder communication and collaboration; organisational culture, cost and contractual constraints; and limitations in tools and technical support, including Building Information Modelling (BIM). The five (5) DOI attributes, namely relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability, are applied to explain why these barriers persist in the post-CDM 2024 Malaysian context. The findings are further cross-validated against the Prevention through Design (PtD) competency framework by Ibrahim et al. (2020), confirming that each barrier cluster corresponds to a core PtD competency element. Overall, this study asserts that DfS success in Malaysia requires a fundamental shift from a culture of minimum compliance to proactive prevention, supported by professional training, mandatory enforcement, and comprehensive digital technology support.

items.title: A study on vocational education students' cognition of human-ai co-creativity: An empirical analysis based on Q methodology
items.abstract: Based on Actor-Network Theory (ANT), this study adopts Q methodology to conduct an empirical exploration of 24 vocational education students, aiming to reveal the internal structure of their cognitive landscape. The experimental results confirm a prominent Middle Collapse phenomenon: the ideal "symmetric co-creative intentionality" is statistically completely absent, and the student group does not form a continuously progressive cognitive spectrum, but presents a drastic structural polarization. The data extract five typical factors, which are clearly divided into two camps: "defensive polarization" (rejecting the status of AI actants to defend subjectivity) and "dependent polarization" (transferring agency to technological black boxes or macro-environments). Topological analysis further shows that there are deep semantic ruptures between different cognitive groups, indicating systemic blockages in the problematization and interessement stages during the "translation" process. The conclusion of this study points out that the current human-AI collaborative cognition of vocational education students does not naturally move toward symbiosis, but is driven by skill-oriented pressure and employment anxiety, falling into an either-or "translation dilemma". This finding reveals the deep cognitive fractures that vocational education faces in cultivating “responsible co-creators” in the intelligent era, and provides key empirical evidence for reconstructing the educational paradigm of human-AI collaboration.

items.title: A Taxonomy of Mental Model Mismatches for Human–Robot Interaction
items.abstract: Mental model mismatches (MMM) in human–robot interaction occur when humans’ internal representations of robots diverge from robots’ actual properties or behaviors, leading to communication breakdowns, task failures, and reduced trust. These mismatches are subtle and difficult to detect, yet the field lacks shared terminology to identify specific types. This makes it difficult to diagnose problems, design targeted interventions, or compare findings across studies. We present a theoretically grounded taxonomy of 16 MMM types organized by the Sense–Plan–Act (SPA) architecture into sensing (7 types), planning (5 types), and acting (4 types). Drawing from cognitive neuroscience, psychology, communication studies, and human factors, each type addresses a distinct cognitive divergence that arises when users apply mechanisms evolved for understanding humans to robotic systems. The taxonomy’s exhaustiveness is established through a dimensional decomposition: three representational dimensions grounded in the neurocognitive architecture of human perception (What, Where, How) are systematically crossed with the three SPA processing stages, and every cell in the resulting matrix is accounted for by a dedicated type or an explicit justification. Each type is equipped with a formal definition and diagnostic examples. We demonstrate the taxonomy’s applicability across two contrasting datasets, TEACh (task-oriented simulation) and SHREC (social therapeutic dialogue), revealing distinct mismatch profiles that reflect the structural differences between the two settings. This taxonomy provides precise terminology enabling researchers to identify specific cognitive mismatches, and a foundation for developing targeted interventions, rather than treating all problems as generic “communication failures.”

items.title: A Teacher Training Model for the Age of AI. Integrating Critical Use and Relational Competences
items.abstract: The spread of artificial intelligence (AI) in educational settings is transforming teaching, learning and the design of school environments (European Commission, 2022; UNESCO, 2023). Alongside the opportunities, questions have emerged regarding the teacher's educational role, which is often overlooked by approaches that focus primarily on AI literacy (Isma'il & Ibrahim, 2025). Against this backdrop, this paper proposes a teacher training model that integrates digital, interpersonal and interpretative competences. The literature highlights how teachers' attitudes towards AI depend not only on their technological skills, but also on the conceptions that shape their professional practice (Cabero-Almenara et al., 2024). Content-transmission approaches tend to be associated with greater resistance to such technologies, whilst perspectives more focused on interpersonal relationships and constructivism interpret them as tools to support learning (Chan & Tsi, 2024). Concerns regarding the spread of AI therefore involve not only technical aspects but also issues of identity linked to the meaning attributed to teaching (Puja et al., 2025). items.title: Advancing Mental Health Support Through Orange Technology and Empathetic Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Mental health systems face a persistent gap in accessible, continuous, and person-centred support. Conversational AI can expand access to psychoeducation, emotional check-ins, self-management, and service navigation, but may also introduce risks of digital exclusion, cultural mismatch, privacy concerns, unsafe advice, and overreliance on automation. This paper develops a conceptual framework integrating Orange Technology, which promotes emotional wellbeing, cultural sensitivity, social connectedness, and resilience, with empathetic AI for mental health support. An integrative literature review examined peer-reviewed systematic reviews and WHO and UN guidance published from 2021 to 2026. Evidence suggests that conversational AI can improve depression, distress, anxiety, and engagement, although effects are heterogeneous and may decline over time. Personalization and empathic interaction may enhance engagement, while the framework's effects on community resilience, cultural sensitivity, and community resource integration require further empirical validation. The framework therefore positions AI as a supportive, human-in-the-loop layer rather than a replacement for clinicians, families, peers, or communities. It connects emotional sensing, empathetic dialogue, personalized support, escalation pathways, community connection, inclusive access, and governance, while aligning mental health innovation with SDG 3, 9, and 17.

items.title: AGENTIC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL FOR IMPROVING OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY AND TRANSFORMING ENTERPRISE BUSINESS MODELS
items.abstract: This article examines agentic artificial intelligence as an emerging class of technologies that fundamentally reshapes business process automation, shifting the paradigm from reactive assistant systems to autonomous solutions capable of independent planning, decision-making, and execution of multi-step actions within defined authority boundaries. The aim of this study stems from a growing realization that traditional AI implementation strategies are failing to deliver expected returns. This discrepancy between strategic ambitions and practical outcomes calls for a systematic investigation of alternative approaches to AI integration, particularly those offering higher autonomy and operational transformation potential. The study demonstrates that agentic AI fundamentally transforms the cost structure of business operations by converting variable labor expenses into predominantly fixed and highly scalable technology costs, thereby altering the economics of enterprise operations. The analysis reveals that organizations implementing agentic AI achieve dramatic operational improvements including task completion time reductions and significant cost optimizations through the elimination of manual inefficiencies. The findings further show that successful scaling of agentic systems depends not so much on technological excellence as on organizational readiness, in particular the development of appropriate governance frameworks for managing autonomous systems, ensuring transparency and explainability in automated decision-making, and integrating AI agents effectively into hybrid human-machine teams while addressing workforce skill gaps. The practical value of this research lies in providing business leaders and technology managers with actionable insights for strategic decision-making regarding AI investments, offering a systematic framework for evaluating deployment opportunities across different business functions, understanding critical success factors that differentiate successful implementations from failed pilots, and anticipating organizational changes required for effective integration. The conclusions provide direction for bridging the persistent gap between AI technological capabilities and practical business outcomes, while outlining promising avenues for future research into economic impact longer-term socioeconomic consequences of widespread AI adoption on workforce composition and organizational structures.

items.title: AI and Gamification for Inclusive and Engaging Learning: A Preliminary Scoping Review
items.abstract: In the current educational landscape, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and gamification are progressively redefining the methods used to design and evaluate learning environments. This contribution proposes an exploratory scoping review aimed at mapping recent literature (2023–2026) on this integration, analysing its implications for inclusion, the personalization of learning pathways, and the transformations of the teacher's role. Furthermore, this study aims to move beyond a merely instrumental view of technological and didactic innovation, framing AI and gamification as educational mediators that require intentional design and methodological coherence regarding the relational and affective dimensions of educational practice. The theoretical framework is structured around three conceptual nodes: AI as a tool for adaptation (through intelligent systems, learning analytics, and generative models); gamification as a lever to promote motivation, active participation, and cognitive engagement; and inclusion as the central interpretive lens. items.title: AI and narratives of the self
items.abstract: The introduction of generative AI into education is more than a technological shift; it poses an epistemological challenge to how knowledge is created, validated, and interpreted in formal settings. In today's hybrid "onlife" context, human-centered agency is essential to navigate an invisible algorithm-driven world. This shift brings both opportunities and tensions, highlighting profound cultural and identity considerations. Bruner conceptualizes education as an interactive process of negotiating meaning rooted in narrative thinking, which contrasts with paradigmatic, logical approaches. Narrative enables the construction of the Self by organizing lived experience into coherent plots. Generative AI, trained on vast linguistic data, fits into this framework as a dynamic dialogic mediator fostering a dialectic between human intention and probabilistic machine response, consistent with Vygotskian cultural mediation and the zone of proximal development. An exploratory questionnaire studied 127 teachers' perceptions of AI's role beyond technological acceptance, examining its mediation of narrative, introspection, creativity, and learner perceptions. items.title: AI facilitation and affective dynamics of online deliberation
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used to facilitate online group discussion, yet their influence on the affective conditions of collective interaction remains poorly understood. Existing research has largely focused on participation, efficiency, or content quality, leaving the emotional dynamics of AI-mediated deliberation underexamined. This paper investigates how AI facilitation relates to the expressed sentiment in online group discussion, understood as one measurable dimension of its affective dynamics. Drawing on two empirical studies conducted in different discussion settings in Afghanistan, one involving a rule-based facilitator and the other a large language model-based facilitator, we analyze differences in expressed sentiment between AI-facilitated and non-AI discussions. Across both datasets, participant sentiment was modestly higher under AI facilitation, although the mixed-effects analyses did not establish statistically significant condition differences. In addition, AI-generated facilitation messages exhibited higher sentiment than participant-authored messages, with a statistically reliable overall gap in both studies and a consistent direction across all five city-specific boards in the first study and all four AI-facilitated groups in the second, suggesting that AI facilitators introduced more positive affective signals into the discussion environment. Rather than treating increased positivity as an unqualified improvement, we interpret these findings as suggesting that AI systems may act as affective mediators, potentially influencing the emotional norms and tone of collective interaction. This raises normative questions about emotional regulation, power, and democratic deliberation, particularly regarding whether affective smoothing may constrain disagreement or reconfigure deliberative agency. By foregrounding affect as a dimension of AI-mediated discussion, this study contributes empirical evidence to debates on the societal implications of AI facilitation and highlights the need for greater attention to the affective norms and expressive patterns introduced by AI facilitation.

items.title: AI Governance: A Comparative Economic Analysis of Japanese and Indonesian AI Regulation
items.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has prompted global discourse on the need for a robust regulatory framework that addresses ethical, legal, and social issues and fosters the innovation through the efficiencies created by AI. This research conducts a comparative analysis of the AI governance frameworks in Japan and Indonesia, examined through the theoretical lens of Economic Analysis of Law (EAL). Japan has taken a nuanced approach that balances the dynamic development of AI with ethical oversight to uphold the Human-Centered AI Social Principles. Indonesia is in the formative stages of developing its AI regulatory environment. Through EAL, this research assesses the efficiency implications of the AI regulatory frameworks between Japan and Indonesia, looking at the implementation of AI in society. By comparing these approaches, this paper highlights the challenges and opportunities for Indonesia in regulating AI technology for the public interest. Indonesia is advised to take a multi-stakeholder approach to build consensus and engage in bilateral cooperation with Japan for the establishment of domestic legislation. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Efficiency; Legislation.

items.abstract: "This study introduces the metaphor of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a 'symbiote' or 'alien organism' (Floridi, 2014), drawing inspiration from the medical domain, where the integration of AI systems into the human body for therapeutic purposes requires a rigorous anthropological selection of suitable subjects."This paradigm offers the opportunity for a rereading of the pedagogical debate on the use of AI in teaching: just as the medical community identifies the subjects compatible with hosting AI for therapeutic purposes, in the same way the education system should identify rigorous and formative criteria for teachers who intend to use this technology for educational purposes. The use of AI in teaching requires a selection based on ethical and anthropological compatibility and a professional evaluation of the teacher, his pedagogical skills, his critical conscience and his educational wisdom and maturity. items.title: AI literacy facets in creative higher education: associations with learning performance and academic well-being
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how students learn, create, and evaluate knowledge in creative higher education, particularly in design-related programmes where students use AI for ideation, prototyping, visual exploration, content generation, and critique. Rather than treating AI literacy as a single global competence, this study conceptualises it as a multidimensional construct comprising AI knowledge, awareness of affordances and limitations, critical reflection, operational ability, ethical awareness, and emotional adaptability. This study examines how these facets relate to learning performance and academic well-being among students in design and related programmes. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 475 students enrolled in design and related programmes across Europe, Asia, and Australia. Data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Three main patterns emerged. First, AI knowledge was positioned as an upstream resource in the theoretically specified model and showed strong positive structural associations with awareness, critical reflection, operational ability, and ethical awareness. Second, learning performance was associated with a “recognise–reflect–produce” pathway, in which awareness and critical reflection helped connect AI knowledge and operational skills with stronger perceived learning outcomes. Third, ethical awareness was more clearly associated with academic well-being than with learning performance, suggesting that ethical clarity around authorship, fairness, bias, and acceptable AI use may support students’ sense of clarity, fairness, and control in AI-supported creative learning. The findings support a knowledge-first, self-regulated, reflective, and ethically transparent approach to AI literacy in design-related creative higher education.
